definition: The practice of splitting documents into retrieval units based on semantic coherence (like topic or section boundaries) rather than a fixed number of characters or tokens.
details: Semantic chunking aims to improve retrieval-augmented generation quality by keeping semantically related content together in the same chunk, rather than arbitrarily cutting sentences or ideas in half.

explainer.lead: Semantic chunking splits documents into retrieval units based on semantic coherence, such as topic or section boundaries, rather than a fixed number of characters or tokens. It aims to improve retrieval-augmented generation quality.

tiers.eli5: Like dividing a book by chapter and topic instead of cutting it every hundred words.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers segment documents at topic or section boundaries before indexing them for retrieval-augmented generation. A pitfall is arbitrary fixed-size cuts that split sentences or ideas in half, which semantic chunking is meant to avoid.
tiers.paperLevel: Documents are partitioned into retrieval units according to semantic coherence rather than a fixed character or token count, keeping semantically related content together. The boundaries depend on how coherence is detected.

explainer.example: A long report is split at section boundaries so each retrieved chunk contains one complete topic instead of being cut mid-sentence.
